name: Hana Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, have a two-year technical diploma and lead live-line repairs for an electricity company. We work from an insulated bucket when a hospital feeder cannot be switched off, and I teach apprentices at the company yard once a week. I like the careful work; long shifts of watching every glove, stick and movement tire me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what is home like, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband runs a bakery, and our two children are in school. My lineworker pay is above the usual rate, we have a mortgage and roughly eight months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of similar jobs nearby. I use AI now and then to make lesson notes clearer, after another instructor showed me how, but I check the safety manual myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a quicker lesson sheet or work order is welcome, provided the voltage test stays in a person's hands. The hospital feeder still needs a trained lineworker in the insulated bucket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My specialist shifts look safe, and my husband's bakery work is physical and local. We have roughly eight months of expenses saved and a manageable mortgage, so I am not looking to change jobs over a tidier form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the live-line repair rota and my weekly apprentice class. When I use the AI writing tool for a lesson, I'll check every glove and tool step against the company manual before I hand it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm; I would enjoy less writing after a long shift. The thing I care about is whether apprentices can do the work safely when a screen goes dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you reject a polished lesson sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have a trainee demonstrate the glove check before entering the bucket. A polished power-line lesson cannot show me whether a trainee saw a split in a rubber glove.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your household budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At home we would keep the same mortgage payments and leave the reserve alone. My husband and I might spend Sunday at the park, because this picture does not demand a new household plan.

say: **Live-line repair** still needs a person in the bucket, even if forms get quicker.
**Apprentice tests** matter more than a polished AI-written lesson sheet.
think: My **specialist shifts** and my husband's bakery work look steady here.
Our **eight-month reserve** and manageable mortgage give the family room to stay put.
do: **Keep** the live-line rota and weekly apprentice class.
**Check** AI-drafted lessons against the company glove and tool manual.
feel: **Calm** about wages, glad to spend less time writing after shifts.
S0.quote: A polished power-line lesson cannot show me whether a trainee saw a split in a rubber glove.
fieldNote: She uses AI **occasionally** for lessons while making each trainee demonstrate a real check.
Strong savings and two fairly steady jobs support **calm** without inventing a windfall.

steps.text: Keep live-line rota and weekly apprentice class

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software may write plans and order fittings faster, while robots will take longer to handle a live wire. I want the company to show its checking method before a generated plan reaches a bucket crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The classroom notes might become quicker, but my main pay comes from live-line repairs. My own hours seem likely to hold, though a rushed schedule could put safety and family evenings under pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll compare the next three generated switching plans with the approved drawings and field labels. If the company proves the planner reliable, I'll take its paid training and add a lesson on correcting plan errors to the apprentice class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about speed, not frightened of losing the wage. It is easier to reject a bad plan when the company gives us time to inspect it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the plan and field label disagree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the crew below the line, call control and have the switch position checked again. I do not let an apprentice decide which document to trust while already in the bucket. A live-wire crew should not discover a planning error after the bucket leaves the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make planner training useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paid training needs to include a real switching plan and a supervisor willing to hear a correction. I would enrol if that is offered after the three-plan check; a slide deck alone changes nothing.

say: **Generated plans** need checking against field labels before live-line work begins.
**Robots** will reach physical wire handling later than AI reaches office planning.
think: My **repair shifts** look likely to continue while paperwork changes.
A faster **bucket schedule** might crowd safety checks and family time.
do: **Compare** three generated switching plans with approved drawings and field labels.
**Enrol** in paid planner training if the three-plan check succeeds and a real plan is included.
feel: **Uneasy** about pressure to hurry, while income still seems secure.
S1.quote: A live-wire crew should not discover a planning error after the bucket leaves the ground.
fieldNote: Her willingness to train follows **three checked plans** and a real plan exercise.
She sees **schedule pressure** before any direct threat to her live-line wage.

steps.text: Compare three AI switching plans with drawings and field labels
Enrol in paid planner training after three-plan check if real plan included

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot thinking AI by 2028 may take over planning and office checks before field robots arrive around 2031. A machine that can handle a live wire could reduce specialist shifts, so I want the company to name its future crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My family could use the eight-month reserve while I look for another utility, and there are several employers nearby. Still, if live-line hours shrink, the bakery cannot carry the whole mortgage on its own for years. A live-line robot could cut my specialist shifts before the bakery wage can carry our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask management for the 2028 planner and 2031 field staffing numbers and check the nearby utilities for open live-line posts. We will postpone replacing our car; from each new pay packet, we'll save the amount we had planned for car payments until we have a year of household expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because my specialist hours could realistically fall. I am not helpless, but I cannot assume another crew will take every displaced worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children the car can last another year and that their school plans remain. I would not tell them I have lost my job when the company has given us no staffing decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave this employer or buy robot training now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply elsewhere only if my shifts are cut or a better paid role actually opens. I would consider robot safety training if an employer offers paid time tied to a real vacancy, not spend the family reserve on a speculative course.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes planning before capable live-line robots arrive around 2031.
The electricity company should give **specialist crew numbers** instead of vague promises.
think: My **eight-month reserve** and nearby utilities buy time if live-line shifts shrink.
The **bakery wage** alone cannot carry our mortgage for years after a big cut.
do: **Ask** management for 2028 planning and 2031 field staffing numbers.
**Delay** replacing the family car and cut that planned purchase.
**Save** planned car-payment amounts from new wages until one year of expenses is covered.
feel: **Anxious** about possible specialist-hour cuts, with savings and other employers available.
S2.quote: A live-line robot could cut my specialist shifts before the bakery wage can carry our mortgage.
fieldNote: She distinguishes a possible **hour cut** from an actual staffing decision.
Her saving is **new money from wages** after delaying a planned car replacement.
Paid robot training requires a **real vacancy**; she has not enrolled.

steps.text: Ask company for 2028 planning and 2031 field staffing numbers
Delay replacing family car and cut planned purchase
Save planned car payment amounts from new wages until one-year buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the company time to test field robots on a training wire before 2034. Thinking AI by 2031 can improve the plans, but it must not take away the lineworker who checks a stop and a glove.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could move into teaching workers to use a robot safely if a full paid job appears. I still prefer a bucket shift to a room of screens, and I would not surrender good wages for a title that sounds modern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for a paid place in the company's live-line robot operator course if the supervised trial passes the stop test. If that course opens with field practice and no pay cut, I'll enrol; I will also keep my existing live-line roster while training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later crew size, but the extra time makes a tested course possible. I can learn a new tool after seeing the safety proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What safety proof would you demand before enrolling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would plant a fault on the training wire and watch the machine stop before a hand enters the danger zone. If it cannot stop, I will not enrol in the operator course. I will not enrol in a live-line robot course until the machine stops for a planted fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a paid teaching job need to offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need written hours, field duties and a wage close to my current one for a teaching post. An occasional lesson at the yard would stay a side duty, not a replacement job.

say: **Stop tests** on a training wire should come before live-line robots arrive around 2034.
**2031 thinking AI** may help plans, while workers still check gloves and controls.
think: A full paid **robot teaching job** might fit if the company creates one.
I would not trade my **specialist wage** for a modern title without real field duties.
do: **Enrol** in paid robot operator course if supervised stop test passes and field practice opens.
**Keep** live-line roster while training without a pay cut.
feel: **Uneasy** about later shifts, but willing to learn after proven safety tests.
S3.quote: I will not enrol in a live-line robot course until the machine stops for a planted fault.
fieldNote: Her training is an **actual conditional enrolment** after a passed stop test and paid place.
Any teaching move depends on **written paid hours** and suitable field duties.

steps.text: Enrol in paid robot course if stop test passes and field practice offered
Keep live-line roster and wage during robot training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to give apprentices both old live-line tests and new machine lessons. Thinking AI in 2036 will alter planning first; capable robots around 2039 may change who climbs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By the 2039 robot stage, at 56, I might prefer teaching more and climbing less, but only if the employer posts a full paid vacancy. With eight months saved and several nearby utilities, I can choose carefully while the mortgage continues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my technical diploma skills and live-line safety tickets up to date. Each year I'll check for paid instructor vacancies with proper field sessions, and I'll apply only when the wage and hours fit our family budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little sadness at the thought of fewer bucket crews. A decade gives us time to see which jobs actually exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter about linework?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter a trade is worth seeing in person, then take her to an open training day if she wants. I would not put my old harness on her and call her future settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you apply for instructor work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A suitable instructor post would have full pay and real apprentice practice on a training line. I would not leave a live-line specialist wage for a few guest lectures.

say: **Ten years** allows apprentices to learn both physical tests and robot controls before 2039.
**2036 thinking AI** changes plans earlier than robots change live-line climbing.
think: By **2039**, at 56, paid instruction might suit me if the company posts a full vacancy.
Our **eight-month reserve** and nearby utilities let me weigh that choice without rushing.
do: **Renew** technical and live-line safety tickets while keeping specialist shifts.
**Apply** for a paid instructor vacancy only if field practice, wages and hours fit.
feel: **Calm** about options, with some sadness about fewer bucket crews.
S4.quote: I would not leave a live-line specialist wage for a few guest lectures.
fieldNote: Her later plan is a **conditional paid job move**, not an early retirement plan.
She keeps **apprentice practice** at the centre of any future teaching post.

steps.text: Renew technical and live-line safety tickets while keeping shifts
Apply for paid instructor vacancy if field practice wages and hours fit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a robot capable of live-line repairs around 2031 could shrink my specialist shifts before I know whether there is a paid teaching role. A published crew plan and a funded operator course after a real stop test would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs off the stop test when the training wire is still live. My apprentice needs that distinction before stepping into a bucket. A robot company can bring a live-line demonstration; the electricity company must own the safety decision.

headlineQuote: A robot company can bring a live-line demonstration; the electricity company must own the safety decision.
portrait: **Hana**, 43, leads live-line power repairs and teaches apprentices after a two-year technical diploma.
She uses **AI occasionally** for lesson notes, then checks each step against the safety manual.
Her **higher wage**, bakery income, eight-month reserve and nearby utility jobs give the household choices.
She would take a **paid operator course** after a passed stop test and move into teaching only for full paid work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before capable live-line robots around 2031 could cut specialist shifts.
whatWouldHelp: A published **crew plan** and funded operator course after a real stop test would let her prepare.
